clue.text: Passionate second eleven ending with victory

parts.note: a team, as in a cricket or football eleven

indicators.note: the ending of the word victory means its final letter only

explanation.surface: A reserve side wins its last match in a heated contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending with victory' takes the last letter of 'victory' to finish the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Steamy describes something heated with sexual desire, so it is a synonym for ardent.

clue.text: Complain, wanting guarantee without question

indicators.note: in its old sense of outside, so the guarantee goes outside the abbreviation

parts.note: a seal is a mark of guarantee, as in a seal of approval

explanation.surface: Someone moans because no warranty is offered and nobody asks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking, so the guarantee wraps the question abbreviation; 'wanting' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To squeal is slang for to protest or grumble loudly.

clue.text: new romance?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held reads only 'new romance? (7)': the start of the clue is missing and there is no scan to restore it, so its wordplay cannot be shown.

clue.text: Blemishes of holy folk? Time to come forward

indicators.note: the letter for time is told to shift to an earlier place in the word for holy folk

parts.note: saints are holy people

explanation.surface: A question whether saints have marks on their record, with a call to step forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to come forward' moves the T of SAINTS from fourth place up to second.
explanation.definitionFit: Stains are marks or blots, so they are synonyms for blemishes.

clue.text: Communications centres left with bits of steel lying round

indicators.note: the rearranged metal letters lie round the word for left, enclosing it
the word steel is broken into bits and reassembled in a new order

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Message hubs left with scraps of metal scattered about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bits of' scrambles the metal word to TELES, and 'lying round' wraps that around the word for left. A teleport is a real telecoms term, not science fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: A teleport is a satellite ground station linking telecommunications networks.

clue.text: Covers thrown with sunrise

indicators.note: the letters are tossed about as if thrown, so they land in a new order

explanation.surface: Bedclothes flung off at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrown' is the anagram signal on SUNRISE; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To insure something is to protect it with a policy against loss, so it covers it.

clue.text: Reliable but unspectacular dismissal

parts.note: in cricket a batter can be out to a catch taken by a dependable fielder, and that fielder is a byword for anyone who does a job steadily

explanation.surface: A dull but dependable way to get someone out.
explanation.walkthrough: A cricket image: a fielder who never drops a catch is said to be this, and the phrase now means any dependable person.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a person trusted to handle something competently without flair, from a fielder sure to hold a catch.

clue.text: Gas from old scientist carrying no weight

indicators.note: the scientist is said to bear none of the weight, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: Isaac Newton, the seventeenth-century English physicist

explanation.surface: Gas from a historic physicist who is light as air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying no' removes W and T, scattered in NEWTON. Fittingly, Newton is linked with weight through gravity.
explanation.definitionFit: Neon is a noble gas, an inert element used in glowing signs.

clue.text: Was the cartoon curate presented with one wicked person?

definitions.text: Was the cartoon curate presented with one

explanation.surface: Asking whether a cartoon clergyman was served something by a villain.
explanation.walkthrough: A famous 1895 Punch cartoon shows a curate served a stale breakfast egg who politely calls it 'good in parts'; hence 'curate's egg'.
explanation.definitionFit: The first is the spoiled food in the cartoon; the second is an idiom for a scoundrel or rogue.

clue.text: Real nudes abandoned protection against the weather

indicators.note: abandoned suggests wild, unrestrained behaviour, so these letters are set loose and rearranged

explanation.surface: Naked people throwing off their inhibitions leave themselves exposed to the elements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoned' is the anagram signal on REALNUDES.
explanation.definitionFit: Underseal is a coating sprayed under a car body to stop rust from rain and road salt.

clue.text: Foreign city with one installed in seat

indicators.note: the numeral is placed inside the piece of furniture, as something fitted in

parts.note: a sofa is a seat
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone abroad is put up on a couch in a foreign capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'installed in' puts I inside SOFA.
explanation.definitionFit: Sofia is the capital of Bulgaria, an example of a city abroad for a British solver.

clue.text: A lot will be seen in this enterprise around university

definitions.text: A lot will be seen in this

indicators.note: the word for enterprise is placed around the abbreviation, enclosing it

parts.note: action, as in taking initiative or a bold undertaking

explanation.surface: A college venture is expected to draw a big crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts ACTION around U. A 'lot' is an item put up for sale in a saleroom, not a large amount.
explanation.definitionFit: Each item offered at a sale by bidding is called a lot, so lots are seen at this kind of sale.

clue.text: Food with a fair amount of fat? That isn't true

definitions.text: Food with a fair amount of fat

explanation.surface: A fatty snack is dismissed as a fib.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is British rhyming slang: 'pork pie' rhymes with 'lie', often shortened to 'porky'.
explanation.definitionFit: The first is a British pastry case of seasoned meat and jelly; the second is rhyming slang for a lie.

clue.text: Now, sir, weddings can turn out to be a sham designed to look good!

definitions.text: a sham designed to look good

indicators.note: the letters are said to turn out differently, so they are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A cynic tells a gentleman that weddings can be mere show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can turn out' signals an anagram of NOWSIRWEDDINGS; 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Window dressing means presentation that hides the truth, a misleading display made to impress.

clue.text: Silly people nicking sailor's jumpers

indicators.note: nicking means stealing, so the fools take the sailor into their midst

parts.note: wallies is British slang for fools
AB is an able-bodied seaman, a sailor; the 's is the link

explanation.surface: Fools steal a sailor's woolly pullovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumpers' looks like British for sweaters but means hopping animals. 'Wally' is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Wallabies are small kangaroo-like marsupials that move by hopping.

clue.text: Fans boo, lots sozzled with ale, when the games are on

indicators.note: sozzled means very drunk, so these letters are mixed up as if staggering

explanation.surface: Drunk supporters jeer, full of beer, during the sporting months.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sozzled' (British slang for drunk) is the anagram signal on FANSBOOLOTS plus ALE; 'with' joins the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The football season is the part of the year when matches are played.

clue.text: A bad person held in fear, not half, is 14

indicators.note: the pieces are placed inside the shortened word, as if held
only half of the word fear is kept, its first two letters

parts.note: a cad is a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: A scoundrel gripped by half-fear is all front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not half' keeps FE of FEAR; 'held in' puts ACAD inside. 14 refers to 14-across, a sham meant to look good.
explanation.definitionFit: A facade is a deceptive outward show, the same idea as a display hiding the truth.

clue.text: At the end of short holiday see Her Majesty wave

indicators.note: the royal letters are placed after the holiday word, at its tail

parts.note: a break is a brief holiday
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's royal cipher

explanation.surface: The Queen is spotted at the end of a short getaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At the end of' puts the royal cipher after the holiday word; 'see' is a link. ER stands for Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: A breaker is a heavy sea wave that breaks into foam on the shore.

clue.text: A game requiring pack of cards to be cut

parts.note: bridge is a card game played with a full pack

explanation.surface: A card game needs the deck cut before dealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' looks like part of the card-game picture but defines the answer; 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To abridge a text is to shorten it, so it is a synonym of trim or shorten.

clue.text: Look to make heartfelt request having changed sides finally

indicators.note: the final letter, standing for left, swaps over to the letter for right

parts.note: to appeal is to plead earnestly

explanation.surface: Trying to look persuasive after switching camps at the last moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having changed sides finally' turns the final L (left) of APPEAL into R (right).
explanation.definitionFit: To appear is to seem, as in 'look tired' or 'appear tired'.

clue.text: Cold hovel leads to artist getting terrible disease

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
a hole is a squalid, dingy dwelling
RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A painter's chilly slum leaves him gravely ill.
explanation.walkthrough: RA = Royal Academician is a crossword staple for an artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Cholera is an acute bacterial infection of the gut that can kill quickly.

clue.text: Political official is taken around a Queen's vessel

indicators.note: the official's title is wrapped around the other pieces, enclosing them

parts.note: a whip is a party official who enforces voting discipline
R is the abbreviation for Regina, Latin for queen, and the possessive adds S

explanation.surface: A party official escorts someone around a monarch's ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is taken around' wraps the whip around the other pieces. R for Regina (Latin for queen) is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A warship is a naval ship built for combat, a kind of seagoing craft.

clue.text: Group of women given gym to mop

parts.note: WI is the Women's Institute, a British women's organisation
PE is physical education, school gym lessons

explanation.surface: A women's club is set gym classes before cleaning up.
explanation.walkthrough: The WI (Women's Institute) is a long-running British community organisation for women.
explanation.definitionFit: To wipe is to clean a surface with a cloth, a synonym of sponge or swab.

clue.text: It's a popular one with cruciverbalists!

definitions.text: It's a popular one with cruciverbalists!

parts.words: It's a popular one with cruciverbalists!
parts.note: crossword fans are said to like 'one', a glass taken at the bar, and the word for it is also an old nickname for the sea, much loved by setters

explanation.surface: A remark about a favourite among crossword solvers.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often clue the sea by this word, and solvers are fond of having one.
explanation.definitionFit: A drink is a serving of something to swallow, and crossword setters also use the word as slang for the sea.

clue.text: Audacity shows lack of judgement — not right

indicators.note: the word for right is to be taken away, as something absent

parts.note: imprudence is rashness, a failure of good sense

explanation.surface: Boldness is shown to be a failure of sense that is morally wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes R from IMPRUDENCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Impudence is cheeky boldness or disrespect, a close synonym of nerve or cheek.

clue.text: Bird — this is hiding by stream

indicators.note: the second word is to be concealed out of sight, so it disappears from the first word

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a rush is a stream or flood, as in a rush of water

explanation.surface: A bird keeps out of sight beside a brook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is hiding' asks the IS in THIS to vanish, leaving TH; 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrush is a songbird, such as the song thrush or mistle thrush.

clue.text: Muscle has fabric around, hurting no end

indicators.note: the fabric word is turned round to face the other way

parts.note: net is an open-mesh fabric

indicators.note: the final letter of the word for hurting is dropped

parts.note: sore means hurting or painful

explanation.surface: An athlete's aching muscle is wrapped in cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' turns the fabric word backwards to TEN; 'no end' cuts the last letter from the word for hurting; 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tensor is a muscle that tightens or stretches a part of the body.
